newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Euro shares gain, German money news aids dlr.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Euro shares gain, German money news aids dlr.

text.p: European share markets advanced on Tuesday morning, boosted by a rebound on Wall Street, but traders were keen to see if U.S. stocks would recover further and preoccupied with interest rate concerns.
"The market was due for a bounce on Wall Street's performance," one London trader said.
"It opened in a blaze of glory...but there's absolutely no volume in this market and no one is going to be interested with all these rate meetings going on," he said.
U.S. monetary policy makers meet later on Tuesday to consider interest rates, while Germany's Bundesbank council has the same mission on Thursday after its summer break.

On the currency market the dollar gained ground against the mark after news of lower-than-expected German M3 money supply growth further dampened speculation that interest rates in Germany would rise in the near future.
Earlier, in another development likely to buoy European share prices, the Bundesbank held its key German money market rate, the repo, steady at three percent.
London's FTSE 100 index of blue chips, which had tumbled 2.5 percent on Friday and slipped another 0.6 percent on Monday, ended the morning below its highs but around 1.1 percent ahead.
Hopes that U.S. and German interest rates will hold steady encouraged institutional investors to return to blue chip issues, dealers said.
"There is a feeling of relief that Wall Street bounced," said Brian O'Donnell, sales trader at Schroders.
"We've got an FOMC meeting and that will tell if we get a rate rise. The answer seems to be no and the market is relaxed," he said.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the policy arm of the U.S. Federal Reserve, meets at 1300 GMT on Tuesday and its decision on interest rates is due at about 1815 GMT.
U.S. economists forecast no change in rates for now as recent data suggest growth is moderate and inflation steady.
Sharing the positive mood in London, Europe's biggest stock market, German stocks gained more than two percent, aided by Wall Street's revival and a stronger dollar -- good news for German exporters.
"Volumes are pretty thin at the moment but I reckon that when they do come in to the market, they will be on the buy side," one Frankfurt broker said.
The Paris bourse also added 1.4 percent in value as confidence returned, while Amsterdam, a star performer on Monday, pushed more than three percent higher.
European dealers were, however, cautious, pondering whether Friday's widespread drop in stock markets marked an end to a relentless rise or just a short-term correction.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 108.70 points (1.41 percent) at 7,803.36 on Monday as investors sought bargains -- reclaiming a chunk of the 247.37 points it lost on Friday in its second bigest points fall ever.
The Dow, a key influence on markets elsewhere, is now 5.5 percent below a record close of 8,259.31 on August 6. But it is nearly 3,200 points or 69 percent above its level two years ago.
Asian markets were in a more sombre mood on Tuesday with Tokyo's Nikkei average falling 88.10 points or 0.42 percent to 18,961.0.

Hong Kong, jolted by signs that speculators will attack its dollar after successful assaults on several southeast Asian currencies, suffered even more. The Hang Seng index closed down 3.85 percent at 15,477.26 points.

In the first key European development of the day, the Bundesbank set a tender for 14-day securities repurchase agreements, or repos, at an unchanged three percent, signalling its monetary policy remained unchanged for now.
Financial markets had expected the rate to be held steady for the moment but speculation that German interest rates will soon head higher has grown.
Markets await Thursday's meeting of the German central bank's council for clues on when to expect a rate move.

The dollar hit a high around 1.84 marks after the Bundesbank said July M3 grew an annualised 5.7 percent from the fourth 1996 quarter, below 6.4 percent in June. Economists had expected money supply to grow 6.3 percent.
"The M3 figures take any pressure away from the Bundesbank to raise German rates soon and, as a consequence, the mark should soften," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.
"The market will still look to Thursday's Bundesbank council meeting but if there ever was a chance of a rate change, it's even slimmer now," he added.
The U.S. currency, meanwhile, topped 118 yen in morning business in London.
CURRENCIES AT 1100 GMT
The dollar was quoted around 1.8355 marks and 118.27 yen, compared with 1.8220 and 117.76 in late European trading on Monday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1100 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE 100 index was up 52.8 points or 1.09 percent at 4,887.8.
FRANKFURT - The DAX index was up 90.89 points, 2.23 percent, at 4,169.49 in floor trade. The IBIS index for electronic trade was 88.68 points, or 2.17 percent, higher at 4,169.23.
PARIS - The CAC-40 index gained 39.32 points or 1.37 percent to 2,909.45.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was quoted around $322.85 an ounce after a morning fix of $322.10, down from Monday's London close of $323.25. Silver was up one cent at $4.53.
